prompt: How many capabilities did a root process in an Alpine container hold by default?
With `--cap-drop ALL`, `chown` failed although the process was still UID 0. Why?

choices.text: The image's files belong to another user
choices.why: The same command worked with the default capabilities.

choices.text: Docker switched the user to `nobody` without saying
choices.why: The process stayed UID 0; only the capabilities changed.

choices.text: `/tmp` was mounted read-only
choices.why: Nothing was read-only in that run.

choices.text: The capability the operation needs was gone
choices.why: Right: `CAP_CHOWN`, not the UID, decides it.

prompt: What does `--security-opt no-new-privileges` add to `--cap-drop ALL`?

choices.text: Setuid programs stop granting privileges
choices.why: Right: no process inside can gain privileges it did not start with.

choices.text: It drops the capabilities a second time, in case the first drop failed
choices.why: It does nothing with capabilities directly.

choices.text: It forbids the container from opening network connections
choices.why: Networking is untouched.

choices.text: It makes the filesystem read-only
choices.why: That is `--read-only`.

prompt: A root process must bind port 80 and nothing else: `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add ___`.
hint: The capability's name, in capitals, without `CAP_`.

prompt: What did `--privileged` give the Alpine container? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every capability the daemon holds, 40 here
choices.why: Yes, against 14 by default.

choices.text: The host's devices, 111 entries in `/dev`
choices.why: Yes, against 14.

choices.text: AppArmor and seccomp switched off
choices.why: Yes, the lesson's other two defaults.

choices.text: A copy of the host's filesystem as its root
choices.why: Its root is still the image; the devices are the danger.

prompt: The `docker:29.8.2-cli` container with the socket mounted listed itself in `docker ps`. What does that show?

choices.text: It ran its own Docker daemon inside
choices.why: The CLI image has no daemon; it asked the host's.

choices.text: It controls the host's daemon, which runs as root
choices.why: Right: it could start any container, privileged included.

choices.text: The socket is read-only, so it can only list
choices.why: A socket is a connection; it does not have a read-only mode for API calls.

choices.text: It sees only containers from its own image
choices.why: It was the only one running; the daemon would list them all.

prompt: `audit.sh` printed `/risky privileged=true caps=[] DOCKER-SOCKET`. What should happen to `risky`?

choices.text: Nothing, since `caps=[]` means no extra capabilities
choices.why: `--privileged` grants them all; `CapAdd` is simply empty.

choices.text: Restart it with `--restart unless-stopped`
choices.why: A restart policy changes nothing about what it holds.

choices.text: Find who needs it; remove both
choices.why: Right: almost nothing needs either, and nothing exposed should have them.

choices.text: Move it to another host
choices.why: It would be root on that one instead.

prompt: A tool's README says to run it with `--privileged`, but it only needs one USB device. What is the narrower grant?

choices.text: `--privileged`, but only for a minute
choices.why: For that minute it holds everything.

choices.text: Mounting the Docker socket instead
choices.why: That is root on the host, not one device.

choices.text: Running it as root without `--privileged`
choices.why: The default set has no access to the host's devices.

choices.text: `--device` for that device
choices.why: Right, and `--cap-add` if one capability turns out to be missing.

prompt: With `--read-only --tmpfs /tmp`, a file written to `/tmp` cannot be executed. Why?

choices.text: The tmpfs is mounted `noexec`
choices.why: Right, with `nosuid` and `nodev` too.

choices.text: tmpfs is in memory, and memory cannot hold programs
choices.why: Programs run from memory all the time; the option decides.

choices.text: `--read-only` applies to `/tmp` as well
choices.why: The file was written; `/tmp` was writable.

choices.text: Alpine has no shell to run it with
choices.why: Alpine has `sh`; the mount refuses execution.

prompt: Postgres with `--read-only` failed on `/var/run/postgresql`. What made it work, with the image still read-only?

choices.text: Removing `--read-only` for Postgres only
choices.why: That gives up the protection instead of keeping it.

choices.text: tmpfs on it and `/tmp`, data on its volume
choices.why: Right: exactly the places its log named.

choices.text: Running it with `--privileged`
choices.why: Privileges do not make a read-only mount writable, and cost everything else.

choices.text: A volume for that directory, named after the container
choices.why: Close, but the socket and lock file are scratch; a tmpfs suits them.

prompt: With `userns-remap` on, what is UID 0 inside a container on the host?

choices.text: Still root, but logged
choices.why: Remapping changes the UID itself.

choices.text: The UID of whoever ran `docker run`
choices.why: That is closer to rootless Podman; remapping uses a range set for the daemon.

choices.text: An unprivileged UID
choices.why: Right: a process past the walls arrives with no rights.

choices.text: UID 65532, like distroless's `nonroot`
choices.why: Unrelated: that is a user inside the image.

prompt: Match each option to what it takes away.

pairs.right: The way back through setuid programs

prompt: A colleague's Compose service for a log shipper has `privileged: true` and mounts `/var/run/docker.sock` "to read container logs". What should Ana ask for?
hint: What does reading logs actually need?

choices.text: Nothing; log shippers always need both
choices.why: Reading log files needs neither.

choices.text: Keep the socket, drop `privileged`
choices.why: The socket alone is still root on the host.

choices.text: Add `read_only: true` to make it safe
choices.why: Read-only does nothing about the socket's power.

choices.text: Read-only mounts of the log files, and neither flag
choices.why: Right: grant what the job needs, which is reading files.
